events.title: A rover mission reaches Mars
events.description: Pathfinder lands carrying the small Sojourner rover.

events.title: The euro begins
events.description: Eleven countries start sharing a currency for financial transactions. Euro notes and coins will arrive later.

events.title: The September 11 attacks
events.description: Terrorist attacks kill thousands of people in the United States. Families, communities and rescuers face devastating losses.

what_happened_next.text:
Apple nearly tripled over five years, while Disney and Nike finished lower. The US basket gained, but less than Apple. A struggling company recovered in this window, yet that does not make every troubled business a bargain. Apple’s path included a very large monthly fall before the end.

Over these years, Pathfinder reached Mars and the euro began for financial transactions. The September 11 attacks caused devastating human losses in 2001. People making decisions in April 1997 could not have known this sequence. The starting page was a snapshot of what they could see, not a summary written with later knowledge.

Apple’s recovery makes a striking contrast with the two other company shares. Yet the chart also contains a very large fall in one month. Recognizing a possible recovery and holding through losses are different challenges. The result is useful because it shows both, rather than turning a well-known company’s later success into a story that was certain from the beginning.

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: Tiger Woods’s victory, executive pay and new technology were prominent stories. Apple’s leadership faced criticism while shareholders struggled.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: Each company followed its own path. The broad basket spread risk across many businesses, even though it did not match Apple’s large gain.
reflection.what_faded_away: An eye-catching executive pay figure did not forecast five-year returns. A sporting victory did not settle the investment outcome of a sponsor.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: The later rankings were unknown. Recognizing Apple’s name today can make its difficult position at the start look less risky than it felt.

hot_stock_outcomes.text: Nike’s famous name did not prevent costly mistakes. Weak demand and heavy discounting hurt earnings in 1998. Then a new planning system caused shortages and late deliveries in 2001, when U.S. shoe sales fell about 4%. Overseas sales were growing, so the business had bright spots, but those gains did not turn this five-year stock result positive.

Disney added attractions, including California Adventure in 2001, but several businesses struggled. Closing its GO.com internet business brought an $878 million charge in 2001. ABC lost viewers and advertising weakened. After September 11, fewer people travelled to Disney’s parks. These problems hurt earnings even while Disney kept opening new places for families to visit.

The iMac’s 1998 launch helped Apple rebuild its computer business and return to an annual profit. Apple then opened its own stores and introduced the iPod in 2001. It sold more than 125,000 iPods in the first two months, and earned $38 million in the 2001 holiday quarter. These were concrete signs of a turnaround behind the strong stock gain.
